questions.question: What is the select statement in Go?
questions.title: Select Statement Basics
questions.direct_answer: select is switch for channels: each case is a channel operation. Blocks until one case is ready, picks RANDOMLY among ready ones. With default: never blocks. With time.After: timeout.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: select is switch for channels: each case is a channel operation. Blocks until one case is ready, picks RANDOMLY among ready ones. With default: never blocks. With time.After: timeout.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
select composes channel operations into one wait:

```go
select {
case msg := <-ch1:
    fmt.Println("from ch1:", msg)
case msg := <-ch2:
    fmt.Println("from ch2:", msg)
case <-time.After(50 * time.Millisecond):
    fmt.Println("timeout")
}
```

Executed: ch2 became ready first (10ms vs 30ms) — select chose it. When MULTIPLE are ready, the choice is RANDOM (fairness — no case starves).

The shape: cases are channel ops — receive (<-ch) or send (ch <- v). select blocks until at least one case can proceed, runs exactly ONE case, then continues.

The three variants:
- default: non-blocking probe (executed: 'nothing ready — didn't block')
- time.After: the timeout pattern (executed: 'timeout fired first')
- for { select { } }: the worker's main loop

The use: a goroutine serving multiple channels — work AND cancellation AND results — is a for/select. Sequential receives would block on the first empty channel; select waits on ALL simultaneously.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    SEL[select] --> C1{case 1 ready?}
    SEL --> C2{case 2 ready?}
    C1 -->|yes| PICK[random pick among ready]
    C2 -->|yes| PICK
    C1 -->|no| W[wait]
    C2 -->|no| W
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanics: select locks ALL its channels (fixed internal order to prevent deadlock between selects), evaluates every case for readiness, picks among ready cases RANDOMLY — the fairness mechanism. Without it, a busy channel 1 would starve channel 2 (first-listed always winning).

The deadlock-free locking: multiple channels locked together atomically — two selects over overlapping channels can't partially acquire and stall.

The default's dual semantics: default with ALL cases not-ready → run default. default with a ready case → the ready case still runs. The common bug: expecting default to interrupt a long-running case — it only answers 'was anything ready RIGHT NOW.'

select{} with no cases: blocks FOREVER — the deliberate permanent-park.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
time.After's channel, mechanically: returns a one-value channel (<-chan Time). A timer in the runtime's heap fires at d, sends one Time, closes the channel. The select case receives the value or observes the close.

The uncollected-timer subtlety: a for/select with time.After(100ms) at 1000 iterations/second creates 100 timers/second holding heap memory for 100ms each — 10 live at a time. Fine. The problem case: time.After(1 * time.Hour) at high frequency — each timer holds memory for an hour.

The context comparison: time.After answers 'this ONE select waited too long.' context.WithTimeout answers 'this WHOLE OPERATION has a deadline' — carried across function calls. Rule of thumb: timeout a channel interaction → select + time.After; timeout a request tree → context.
